stemBlocks.value: In triangle OAB, M is the midpoint of OA and N is the midpoint of OB, with OA = a and OB = b. (a) Express OM and ON in terms of a and b. (b) Show that MN = ½(b − a). (c) State TWO geometric relationships between MN and AB.
Think first: Halving each side from O gives the two midpoints immediately, and the segment joining them is just the difference of those halves.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p189-q16 from workbook page 189.

solutionSteps.instruction: Halve OA and OB to reach the two midpoints.

contentBlocks.value: M is halfway along OA and N is halfway along OB.

solutionSteps.instruction: Route the journey from M to N through O.
Write AB in terms of a and b.

contentBlocks.value: MN = ½AB, a scalar multiple, so the two segments point the same way.
Result: MN is parallel to AB and half its length

strategyBlocks.value: Write OM and ON as halves of a and b, form MN = ON − OM, then compare the result with AB = b − a.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) OM = ½a and ON = ½b  (b) MN = MO + ON = −½a + ½b = ½(b − a)  (c) MN is parallel to AB, and MN is half the length of AB.

whyThisWorks.value: When one vector is a scalar multiple of another, the two line segments must be parallel, and the size of the scalar gives the ratio of their lengths. Here the scalar is ½, so MN is parallel to AB and exactly half as long. This is the midpoint theorem, proved by algebra rather than by congruent triangles.

commonErrors.misconception: Writing MN = ½a − ½b by taking the journey in the wrong direction.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Writing MN = ½a − ½b by taking the journey in the wrong direction.

commonErrors.misconception: Saying MN equals AB because both are ½(b − a) in form, ignoring the factor.

promptBlocks.value: In the same triangle, P is the midpoint of AB. Express MP in terms of a and b.

answerSpec.displayValue: OP = ½(a + b), so MP = OP − OM = ½(a + b) − ½a = ½b
acceptedForms: OP = ½(a + b), so MP = OP − OM = ½(a + b) − ½a = ½b
